lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- They Told Me Something Else
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Veridiana Sterman Petrilli | Lesson 9 -- They Told Me Something Else
lesson.grammar_point: reported speech with say and tell

listenings.text: I train front-desk teams, and there is one sentence I ask every new person to learn in the first week. It is not an apology. It is a question: who told you that, and when? Because almost every angry conversation at a desk is not really about the problem. It is about two people holding two different versions of the same fact, and neither of them knowing where the other version came from. Now, the same thing works from your side of the desk, and travellers almost never use it. If you were told something, say who told you and say it in their words. The woman on the phone told me the tour left at nine. That single sentence does three things at once. It shows the person in front of you that you are not inventing it. It gives them somebody to check with. And, this is the important part, it is not an accusation, because you are quoting, not arguing. The version that goes wrong is the one that starts with you people. The version that works starts with somebody told me. And if you can add when, you have handed them the whole problem in one line, and they can fix it in about twenty seconds.

I run day trips out of Miami, and I want to explain why you get three different answers to the same question, because it is almost never anybody lying to you. Our morning boat moves from nine to ten thirty in October, when the season changes. The phone team gets the new time on the first of the month. The website gets it when somebody remembers to edit the page, which can be a week later. And the drivers hear it from us on the morning it changes, which is why a driver may still be telling people about last week. Three sources, three ages of the same fact. So here is what I would ask for if I were you, and it is three things. Ask for a name, so you know who said it. Ask for a time, not soon and not later, an actual number. And ask for one line of it in writing, by message or by email, because writing is the only version that does not change when the shift changes. Do that once, at the start, and you will not have to ask anybody again.
